name: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown

inherit.field: setup: lean back only slightly (about 30 degrees at most), no extra lean during the pull
inherit.why: true for this child because the seat, pad and overhead pulley are the parent's; the coach sources here add that the torso must also not lean into each rep or twist (c6, c11).

claims.text: On the pulldown machine: clip on a single handle, stand to take it, then sit with the thighs tight under the pads.

quotes.text: Attach a single handle attachment to the lat pulldown machine.
Stand up to grip the attachment, before taking a seat, making sure your thighs are tightly secured underneath the pads.

claims.text: Pull the elbow back and down toward the back pocket until the handle just passes chin height.

quotes.text: Pull the attachment towards your upper chest by pulling your elbow back and down towards your back pocket. Pull the attachment towards your upper chest until it just passes chin height.

claims.text: Start by dropping the shoulder away from the ear, then pull the elbow down until the upper arm is flush with the side.

quotes.text: Brace your core and set your scapula, then drive straight downward, leading by dropping your shoulder away from your ear and then following through by pulling your elbow downward until your upper arm is flush with your torso.

claims.text: Pause briefly at the bottom, keep tension on the way up, and let the cable lift the shoulder toward the ear at the top.

quotes.text: Once you reach the end of the range of motion, pause for a beat and then reverse the movement. Maintain continuous tension with the cable as you let your elbow rise. At the top, allow the cable to pull your shoulder upward towards your ear.

claims.text: Return slowly, letting the cable take the handle back up.

quotes.text: Reverse the movement by slowly extending the arms, allowing the cable to pull the attachment back up.

claims.text: The trunk must work to stop the torso twisting; if it swings or twists, lower the load.

quotes.text: The core must work hard in a single arm lat pulldown to prevent the torso from twisting. If you find your torso swings or twists, lower the load – this helps to keep the tension on the back.

claims.text: The obliques work to keep the torso upright and untwisted (coach source).

quotes.text: There is also more involvement from the core, particularly the obliques, as they must work to keep the torso upright and prevent it from twisting.

claims.text: It works the lats, biceps, rhomboids and traps (coach source).

quotes.text: The single arm lat pulldown works the lats, biceps, rhomboids, and traps.

claims.text: Expect to use less than half of your two-arm pulldown weight per arm.

quotes.text: While you typically have to use a lighter load than 50% of what you can pull with bilateral lat pulldowns due to instability

claims.text: At the end of the pull the elbow can only go backward, and the shoulder may roll forward; the coach source says this compensation may cause stress or discomfort.

quotes.text: Once you’ve reached the end of the range of motion, your elbow has nowhere to go but backwards. As a result, your shoulder might start to move forward. This compensation may cause undue stress or discomfort.
quotes.where: Common Single-Arm Lat Pulldown Mistakes: Dumping Your Shoulders Forward

claims.text: Leaning into each rep to get the arm down is a fault; brace the abs harder instead.

quotes.text: If you find yourself leaning into each repetition to get your arm where it needs to be, try contracting your abs harder to stabilize your spine.
quotes.where: Common Single-Arm Lat Pulldown Mistakes: Torso Twisting

claims.text: Setups vary: seated facing the machine, seated sideways, or kneeling at a cable machine.

quotes.text: If you have access to a lat pulldown machine, you can start in a seated position, or seated sideways, working your arm farthest from the pulley system.
Grip the attachment, before adopting a kneeling position on the floor.
Attach a single handle attachment to the cable machine.

claims.text: Stop pulling once the elbows stop moving down and start moving back; ACE says further pulling adds stress to the shoulder joint. Written for the two-arm bar pulldown; applied to one arm because the elbow path is the same.

quotes.text: Continue pulling until the bar nears or touches your chest, or more importantly, you observe your elbows no longer moving downward, but now beginning to move backwards.
Avoid any further pulling as this places additiomnal stresses into the shoulder joint.

claims.text: The plate uses a 2-second pull and a 2-second return (the cadence Lusk 2010 tested on two-arm pulldowns) with a brief pause at the bottom; a study protocol and coach cue, not a tested recommendation. BarBend gives no seconds for the pause, so the 1 s on the plate is a drawing convention (LR-33).

quotes.text: Participants maintained a cadence of 2-second concentric and 2-second eccentric phases.
Once you reach the end of the range of motion, pause for a beat and then reverse the movement.

claims.text: In 20 healthy adults squeezing a hand dynamometer, grip was strongest with the wrist in the position they chose themselves (about 35 degrees bent back) and weaker when the wrist was moved 10 to 15 degrees away from it in any direction, including curled forward (flexion). Applied to holding a bar or handle by reasoning, not measured on this exercise.

quotes.text: Grip strength and wrist position were recorded in the self-selected position and then again while the subjects voluntarily deviated the wrist randomly into flexion, extension, or radial or ulnar deviation of 10 to 15 degrees.
The self-selected position was 35 degrees of extension and 7 degrees of ulnar deviation.
Grip strength was significantly less in any position of deviation from this self-selected position, even after accounting for fatigue.

claims.text: Thumbs go around the handle: a general grip drill for all grips, applied to the cable handle by inference (not a pulldown text).

quotes.text: Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar.

sources.title: How to Do the Single-Arm Lat Pulldown for Spectacular Back Development (BarBend)
Grip width and forearm orientation effects on muscle activity during the lat pull-down (Lusk, Hale, Russell, J Strength Cond Res)
The relationship between wrist position, grasp size, and grip strength (O'Driscoll et al., J Hand Surg Am)
Single Arm Lat Pulldown (PureGym exercise guide)
Grip selection and location, excerpt from Weight Training: Steps to Success, 5th ed. (Baechle and Earle, Human Kinetics)

plate.viewWhy: The elbow path down to the side and the shoulder rolling forward read from the side. The torso twist (c6) is a rotation the engine cannot draw.
plate.equipment: Lat pulldown station as the parent plate, with a single handle (singleHandle) on the cable (c1).
plate.start: Seated facing the machine, thighs tight under the pad (c1); working arm straight overhead holding the handle, shoulder lifted toward the ear by the cable (c4); torso upright (c7).
plate.end: Handle just past chin height, elbow down and back toward the back pocket, upper arm flush with the side (c2, c3); shoulder down, not rolled forward (c10).

checkpoints.label: Shoulder down first
checkpoints.what: Drop the shoulder away from the ear before the elbow bends.

checkpoints.label: Elbow to pocket
checkpoints.what: Elbow pulls back and down toward the back pocket, handle just past the chin.

mistake.what: Pulling past the end: the elbow drives backward behind the body and the shoulder rolls forward.
mistake.why: The coach source names this compensation and says it may cause stress or discomfort; ACE says to stop when the elbows start moving back. Frequency is not measured.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: no frequency word for a fault (BarBend's "perfectly common" is about one side being stronger; "usually" and "frequently" there, and PureGym's "typically", are about muscles, athletes or the load). LR-31 step 2: the past-end pull is the only named fault a quote ties to harm (c10; ACE c13, two-arm pulldown, MECH), and it is first in BarBend's common-mistakes list. BarBend's Going Too Heavy (a load choice) and Torso Twisting with the lean (c11), and the PureGym twist tip (c6), state no harm; if ACE's closing stress line is read onto the backward lean, the past-end pull still wins on harm sources (c10, c13).

tells.text: Upper arm flush with your side

plate.variantLine: Drawn: seated facing the pulldown machine with a single handle (c1). The kneeling cable-column setup (c12) shares the elbow path, stop point and anti-twist claims (c2, c3, c6, c10, c13); only the thigh-pad claim (c1) is machine-only.

grip.type: Single handle (c1). Neither technique source names a palm direction, so none is sourced here.
grip.width: One hand, set by the handle.
grip.thumb: Wrapped around the handle (c16). The thumb-over option is not used: no claim supports it.
grip.handContact: Not sourced; drawing convention (LR-4): the hand is drawn with the handle across the base of the fingers.

setup.step: Clip a single handle to the cable.
Stand to take the handle, then sit with your thighs tight under the pads.
Use less than half your two-arm pulldown weight to start.
Brace your trunk so it won't twist.
No pulldown machine? Kneel at a cable machine.

posture.point: Thighs pinned; torso upright and square.
Drop the shoulder away from the ear first.
Elbow back and down toward the back pocket, upper arm flush with the side.
Stop when the handle passes the chin and the elbow stops moving down.
Brief pause, then a slow return; the cable lifts the shoulder at the top.
No leaning or twisting into the rep.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Pulling past the end so the elbow goes behind you and the shoulder rolls forward.
handlingMistakes.fix: Stop when the handle just passes your chin.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Twisting or swinging the torso to finish the rep.
handlingMistakes.fix: Brace the trunk. If it still twists, lower the load.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Leaning into each rep to get the arm down.
handlingMistakes.fix: Tighten your abs to hold the spine still. If your torso still swings or twists, lower the load.

rows.means: Expected: the obliques keep your torso from twisting.
rows.fix: Nothing to fix. If you start to twist, lower the load.

rows.means: Usually means you pull past the end and the shoulder rolls forward.
rows.fix: Stop when the handle passes your chin.

risks.risk: Shoulder stress from rolling the shoulder forward at the end of the pull.

zooms.right: Upper arm flush with the side, shoulder down.
zooms.wrong: Elbow behind the body, shoulder rolled forward.

zooms.right: Arm long overhead, the cable lifting the shoulder toward the ear, tension kept on the handle.
zooms.wrong: Handle let fly up with no tension.

add.why: Coach source lists the rhomboids and traps (c8).
Coach source: the obliques stop the torso twisting (c7).

libraryDiff.why: lats primary and biceps secondary stand (c8). No EMG study of the one-arm pulldown was found, so the additions rest on coach sources only.

notes: No peer-reviewed study of the single-arm pulldown was found (PubMed searches for unilateral/one-arm pulldown returned nothing relevant). BarBend's guide was read in full as a second technique source. No source names the palm direction on the single handle, so the grip type is left open rather than invented. The back feel row was dropped: no source links a back or one-sided ache to leaning or twisting. c7 and c8 rest on one coach source (WEAK).

LR-32 (W2-50, supervisor 2026-10-18): the quotes cannot show which fault is most common. Under LR-31 the past-end pull is the top fault (first in BarBend's list, the only fault with stated harm), so drawable stays true and handlingMistakes starts with it. census.json's 'defining fault is a sideways lean' has no source.

LR-34 check (W2-53, 2026-10-18) against cards/lat_pulldown.json and verified shared cards on head 5036283d; shipped sheet tools/plates/layers/exercises/lat_pulldown.howto.mjs on main b99a9e25. Thumb fails: the parent sources only thumbs around the bar (c4, c13) and lists an open grip as an error (c13), so the thumb-over option has no support; way (1): Baechle and Earle's "Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar." is this card's c16 (MECH). Pin and start lighter fails: the shipped 'Push the pin fully in. Start light.' has no claim for 'start light' on the parent or a shared card; the pin line stays sourced for this card by shared/selector-pin.json c1, whose appliesTo lists it. 'Start lighter' is stated by this card's own c9 (setup[2]). Lean holds: lat_pulldown c2 and c3, restating the setup string 'Lean back slightly, about 30 degrees at most.' One inherit entry is left.
